reference_title: Drilled Shafts: Construction Procedures and LRFD Design Methods

sections.title: Introduction
sections.body: Post-construction integrity testing plays an integral role in the drilled shaft design and construction process. Most common purpose: quality assurance of concrete placement — measure characteristic of hardened concrete to assess integrity. Non-destructive integrity tests (NDT) have no permanent effect on the shaft; interpretation is non-destructive evaluation (NDE). NDE must be viewed within context of well-designed inspection process — NOT a substitute for quality construction or inspection. Second application: evaluate shafts when defect is suspected based on construction observations, anomalous cylinder tests, or unexpected performance. May include destructive methods (coring). Two categories of post-construction tests: (1) planned tests as part of QA procedure — non-destructive, relatively inexpensive, routine on US transportation projects; (2) unplanned tests as part of forensic investigation — more time-consuming and expensive, requires more extensive evaluation. ASTM D6760 definitions: anomaly — irregularity in NDT results indicating possible flaw; flaw — deviation from planned shape or material characteristics; defect — flaw that may significantly detract from drilled shaft performance.
key_points: NDT/NDE: non-destructive integrity tests — quality assurance of concrete placement
NDE is NOT a substitute for quality construction and inspection
Planned tests: routine QA; Unplanned tests: forensic investigation of suspected defects
Anomaly → Flaw → Defect: increasing severity in ASTM D6760 terminology
Defect: flaw that may significantly detract from performance
sections.applicability: Post-construction integrity testing and QA for all drilled shaft projects

sections.title: Non-Destructive Integrity Tests
sections.body: Most common NDT methods: (1) Crosshole Sonic Logging (CSL) — most widely used QA method; ASTM D6760; vertical access tubes cast in shaft; acoustic transmitter and receiver pulled upward simultaneously at same elevation (zero-offset); measures signal travel time (First Arrival Time = FAT) and signal strength (Relative Energy = RE); theoretical wave velocity Vc = √(αE/ρ); strong anomaly = increase in FAT + decrease in RE; one tube per foot of diameter minimum; tubes must be water-filled; advantages: relatively accurate and low cost; effective for anomalies in core concrete; limitations: difficulty locating defects outside line-of-sight between tubes; (2) Thermal Integrity Profiling (TIP) — ASTM D7949; temperature cables or access tubes cast in shaft; monitors temperature profile generated by heat of hydration during concrete cure; low temperature zones indicate potential defects; capable of capturing anomalies anywhere in cross section including outside reinforcement cage; relatively accurate, low cost, fast; limited time window for measurements; limited effectiveness at tip; (3) Gamma-Gamma (GG) — Caltrans Test 233; radioactive source and detector in single probe lowered into access tubes; backscattered gamma rays correlate to concrete density; effective for anomalies around shaft perimeter; requires radioactive material handling; anomaly detection limited to several inches from tubes; (4) Sonic echo (Pile Integrity Test, PIT) — impact at shaft top generates compressive wave; reflections measured; estimates shaft length and identifies major anomalies; no access tubes required; most effective for relatively short, slender shafts; less effective in stiff soils; pile integrity tester: ASTM D5882. Requires expert knowledge for interpretation. Technician performs field test; qualified engineer interprets results. All require specialized software.
key_points: CSL (ASTM D6760): most widely used; one access tube per foot of diameter; water-filled tubes required
CSL anomaly: increase in First Arrival Time (FAT) + decrease in Relative Energy (RE)
TIP (ASTM D7949): temperature during heat of hydration; captures anomalies anywhere in cross section
Gamma-Gamma: single-tube; backscattered gamma rays; anomalies within inches of tubes
Sonic Echo (PIT, ASTM D5882): no tubes; surface impact; for relatively short slender shafts
All NDT requires expert interpretation; technician for field work, qualified engineer for interpretation
equations: Eq. 16-1: Vc = √(αE/ρ) — theoretical compressional wave velocity in concrete
Eq. 16-2: α = (1-ν)/[(1+ν)(1-2ν)] — constraint factor for compressional wave
Eq. 16-3: ρ = γ/g — mass density of concrete

sections.title: Thermal Method (TIP)
sections.body: Thermal Integrity Profiling (TIP) measures temperature generated during concrete heat of hydration to infer shaft geometry and identify defects. Thermal sensors (thermocouples or other temperature-measuring devices) embedded in shaft via cables attached to rebar cage or via access tubes. Multiple sensors at different radial positions provide information on shaft geometry. Low temperature at a given depth indicates low concrete mass — possible void, neck, or soil inclusion. High temperature indicates possible bulge or overbreak. Measurements taken during early curing period (typically 12-72 hours after concrete placement). TIP is particularly effective for identifying anomalies outside the reinforcing cage — a key limitation of CSL testing. ASTM D7949 for TIP with access tubes; additional methods use wire cables. Can also detect anomalies at the shaft tip where CSL is less effective.
key_points: TIP detects anomalies anywhere in cross section including outside reinforcing cage
Low temperature at depth: low concrete mass — possible void, neck, or soil inclusion
High temperature: possible bulge or overbreak
Measurement window: typically 12-72 hours after concrete placement
Effective at shaft tip where CSL is limited
ASTM D7949; thermal cables attached to rebar cage or via access tubes
sections.applicability: Post-construction QA; anomaly detection outside reinforcing cage and at shaft tip

sections.title: Drilling and Coring
sections.body: When NDT indicates potential defect, or when more definitive information is needed, physical investigation by coring or drilling may be performed. Concrete coring: NX size or larger cores drilled through suspicious zone; cores examined visually for defects; compressive strength tests of cores from suspicious and comparison zones. Downhole video inspection: camera lowered into drill hole to visually inspect core hole, access tube hole, or casing; provides direct observation of concrete quality, soil inclusions, and borehole conditions; valuable when NDT anomalies are ambiguous. Crosshole sonic tomography: full-waveform tomographic reconstruction of anomaly shape and size from multiple CSL profiles between all available tube combinations. Advantages of physical investigation: direct visual evidence; definitive determination of defect presence, size, and character. Limitations: costly; may further damage shaft or introduce new defects; may not be justified for minor anomalies.
key_points: Concrete coring: direct visual inspection plus compressive strength tests for suspected defect zones
Downhole video: visual inspection of core holes, access tubes, or casings
Crosshole sonic tomography: full-waveform reconstruction of anomaly shape and size
Physical investigation provides definitive confirmation but is costly and may damage shaft
sections.applicability: Investigation of suspected defects identified by NDT

sections.title: Load Testing for Drilled Shaft Integrity Evaluation
sections.body: In some cases, load testing may be performed specifically to evaluate the structural or geotechnical integrity of a shaft suspected to have a defect. Proof testing per Chapter 13 can demonstrate whether a shaft with a suspected defect can still meet required performance criteria. If the defect is structural (below bearing capacity of concrete), a proof test demonstrating adequate geotechnical resistance at loads below the structural capacity provides useful information. High strain dynamic testing may detect structural defects through wave mechanics analysis. A lateral load test provides information on structural integrity in flexure — however, large lateral loads on production shafts may cause permanent structural damage and non-recoverable displacement.
key_points: Proof test can demonstrate adequate performance despite suspected defect
High strain dynamic test may detect structural defects through wave analysis
Lateral proof test for structural integrity — risk of permanent damage to production shaft
sections.applicability: Quality assurance testing for shafts with suspected defects

sections.title: Summary
sections.body: Chapter described non-destructive integrity testing methods for drilled shafts: CSL, TIP, Gamma-Gamma, and Sonic Echo; physical investigation methods (coring, video); and use of load testing for integrity evaluation. NDE is a key quality assurance tool but not a substitute for quality construction and inspection. CSL is most widely used; TIP provides complementary information especially outside the reinforcement cage. Assessment and acceptance using NDE results described in Chapter 17.
